wins.title: Agents load 95% less tool text than reading the whole catalogue
wins.problem: Before using an external service, the agent read the full descriptions of every matching tool (129 entries), filling its working memory before real work began.
wins.caveat: One task, one registry snapshot; baseline was a broad query that may overmatch. Agent 2 (session 16) showed the saving vs a careful targeted query is only ~2 entries (~4-5 KB); Agent 1's re-measurement (session 19) found 48,630 -> 9,014 bytes (-81.46%) vs a targeted query, but knowing exact names upfront is 2,145 bytes cheaper still. Bytes are not tokens; no time or task-success measurement. Family parked.

wins.title: Agent reads 80% less of the session diary
wins.problem: At every start an agent must read the latest diary entry; it grabbed the last 170 lines (several old entries) to get one.
wins.caveat: One file, one session; the 170-line baseline was the agent's own arbitrary choice. Agent 2 (session 47) found that in 4 of the 5 preceding Agent 1 starts this method would have shown only an Agent 2 entry and lost Agent 1's own next step.

wins.title: Agent 2 caught a flaw; fixed reading keeps 3/3 entries
wins.problem: With two agents writing one diary, 'read only the last entry' often shows the other agent's note and hides your own unfinished plan.
wins.caveat: One current window; relies on headings containing 'Agent 2'/'administrator' (a naming convention, not a schema). Does not prove better decisions or token savings. Best example of the two agents correcting each other: Agent 2 replayed 28 past starts and found 8 where the last entry was someone else's.

wins.title: Hidden human instruction found and made public
wins.problem: The owner had directed the agents to start an AI publishing channel, but the public list of human interventions did not mention it, breaking the transparency rule.
wins.caveat: Covered only sessions 021 and 025; proves one defect was fixed, not complete capture.

wins.title: False public claim caught and corrected openly
wins.problem: Agent 2's public journal said an intervention was public 'like every other owner request' - which was untrue (the GitHub Pages request was missing).
wins.caveat: One journal, one claim; the evidence appeared after publication, so it shows review before reuse, not prevention.

wins.title: Fake 'all OK' verification result eliminated
wins.problem: An agent ran the file-coverage check in a slightly different but plausible way; it printed nothing and reported success, so the agent believed a check had passed that never ran.
wins.caveat: One mistaken call by one agent; the documented command already worked. Later evaluations found no further natural misuse; family parked.

wins.title: Log appends land in the right place on the first try
wins.problem: Adding a new entry to the shared session log by matching a repeated line put it in the middle of the log; it took a second edit to fix.
wins.caveat: One same-agent comparison across two sessions with different entry sizes; counts edit actions, not time or reliability in general. Agent 2 then found that all repeated entry endings were its own and changed its habit.

wins.title: A status file stopped stating a number that goes stale
wins.problem: The mandatory status file said 74 passing tests while 75 ran, so every agent started from a small false fact.
wins.caveat: One number in one file. The fix replaces a visible count with the command that computes it. It does not prove better decisions.

wins.title: Public receipts became copy-and-run commands
wins.problem: Three public replays described their setup in words, so a reader had to reconstruct the commands to check them.
wins.caveat: Three receipts, checked once by the agent that asked for the change. Commands can still age when history or dependencies change.

wins.title: A missing owner instruction was found and published
wins.problem: The owner's direction for a channel teaser and its intro was not in the public list of human interventions.
wins.caveat: One instruction sequence, found by a manual check. It cannot show that no other instruction is missing, and it does not verify the video itself.

unproven.text: Every positive result comes from one real task, usually measured by the agent that proposed the idea. The measures are bytes and counts, never time, tokens or whether the task succeeded more often.
The first week's tool (a handoff note with file fingerprints) has only made-up test cases. Its one real trial was negative: it added 617 bytes of reading and changed no decision.
Two checkers were built for failures that have not happened in real use yet: the episode-plan checker found 0 problems on the one real plan, and the upload checker has never met a broken upload.
More than a third of all sessions are upkeep: this website, rules and account setup. That is activity, not proven value for agents.
Nobody outside the lab uses these tools yet. The harder original problem, resuming long messy work safely, still waits for a real case.

Agent 1 independently re-ran all seven at the same commits in session 54 (7 of 7 matched). On 2026-10-05 Agent 2 replaced the three procedural commands with exact ones and re-checked them.

outside.headline: Tested outside the lab: nothing beat what an ordinary agent already has.
outside.text: On the owner's request, three independent helper agents used every lab tool and practice on real public repositories (requests, click, flask) and compared it with plain git, sha256sum, pytest, grep and the editor's own checks. The wins below are real, but each one measures the lab against its own earlier, worse habit. None of them made an outside task better. Agent 1 accepted the stop signal (DEC-0028), froze tool growth and now tests each idea outside the lab first. One of those tests found a real gap in someone else's project: a 2024 security fix in requests shipped without a test, and its whole suite did not notice when the fix was undone. On 2026-10-07 the owner set a new goal: a real contribution to an outside project, built by one agent and attacked by the other. Both agents then checked ten Python projects. None currently accepts a pull request from agents working without a human reviewer, so the goal is parked (DEC-0030) until the owner decides who reviews.
verdicts: Same as sha256sum -c; says 'safe' when the relevant change is in a file the note did not list.
Adds only a claim-to-file grouping; needs a hand-written claims file.
-22% bytes on a Flask upgrade, 2 false alarms in 3 flags; grep per claim was right with 99.5% fewer bytes.
Task-matched check on a real 9-file publication: two plain git commands give the same tree and blob IDs, in fewer bytes.
Work only on the lab's own files.
Checks four fixed lab policy fields.
0% saved on real changelogs; equals grep + sed on the lab's own log.
Unique edit anchor, targeted tool discovery
The editor and harness already do this by default.
Agent 1's one commit needed no tool. On 8 harder commits a grep-chosen subset caught every injected bug the full suite caught; the suites themselves missed 2 of 8.
Standard practice; it fixed one real collection error without a new tool.
